entities.summary:
Heraldry is the study, or art of creating, granting, and blazoning arms and ruling on questions of rank or protocol. This medieval discipline originated in the 12th century among the knights of Europe, particularly in England, France, and Scotland. The first recorded use of heraldry dates back to 1135, during the reign of King Henry I of England. Over time, heraldry became an integral part of the nobility's armorial bearings, serving as a visual representation of their family, status, and allegiances. The use of heraldry was not limited to the nobility, as it was also adopted by the rising middle class and eventually became a popular form of artistic expression. Despite its origins in the Middle Ages, heraldry continues to influence modern-day symbolism and visual identity.

Heraldry played a significant role in the development of coats of arms, which were first used in the 14th century. These unique identifiers became essential for identifying individuals, families, and institutions, and their design and display were governed by complex rules and conventions. The creation of coats of arms was often a time-consuming and costly process, requiring the expertise of professional heralds and the use of expensive materials. As a result, heraldry became a status symbol, reflecting the wealth, power, and prestige of the individuals and families who wore them.

One of the most significant consequences of heraldry was the standardization of national identity. The use of coats of arms and other heraldic symbols became a unifying force among nations, reflecting their unique history, culture, and values. The adoption of heraldry as a national symbol helped to create a sense of shared identity and purpose, which was essential for the development of modern nations. Today, heraldry continues to play an important role in national identity, with many countries using their coats of arms as official symbols of state.
